summary: Cumberland Head Light on Lake Champlain near Plattsburgh: an 1838 light whose stone tower dates from 1868, discontinued in 1934, returned to the tower in 2003; private property.

lens.note: Fourth-order Fresnel installed 1856 (LighthouseFriends); placed in the 1868 tower; fixed white in 1856 per LighthouseFriends

structures.note: Fifty-foot conical tower (LighthouseFriends); USLHS place record gives tower height 50 ft. The first tower of 1837-38 was taken down in 1867.
Forty feet, battery-operated light, placed between the stone tower and the lakeshore (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Private property. USLHS place record: Open to Public: No.

events.note: First tower, thirty feet of rubble limestone, built by Peter Comstock for $3,325
First light shown from the first tower, 1838
New lantern room and fourth-order Fresnel lens with a fixed-white light
First tower disassembled; its stone reused for the new tower
Fifty-foot conical stone tower built on a new site; light first exhibited 1 November 1868
Congress appropriated $3,000 to buy fifteen acres and clear the trees that hid the light; a further $250 in 1879
Emma D. Tabberrah appointed keeper on 19 December 1904 after her husband's death
Keeper William H. Fido assisted a disabled motor boat, brought its occupants ashore and repaired the boat (Commissioner's report, fiscal 1921)
Forty-foot steel skeletal tower with battery light replaced the stone light
Land subdivided and offered at auction
Private family moved into the abandoned keeper's house under a World War II veterans' land program
Town of Plattsburgh put a drawing of the lighthouse on its official seal
Property sold to another private owner
Light returned to the limestone tower in March 2003 with the help of the owners (Coast Guard)

corrections.why: The record's 1838 date belongs to the first tower of 1837-38, which was taken down in 1867. The standing conical limestone tower was built and first lit in 1868 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS place record 'Year Tower Established: 1868').

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Two towers. The first light shone from the 1837-38 tower; the standing stone tower was first lit on 1 November 1868 (LighthouseFriends). The record's 1868 'first lit' and 1838 'first lit' are both true of different towers.

The stone light was discontinued in 1934 when a forty-foot steel skeletal tower took over (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 'Year Discontinued: 1934'). The 2003 date in other sources matches the return of the light to the stone tower in March 2003 (LighthouseFriends). LighthouseFriends does not say what became of the steel tower.

notes_for_editor: (1) Focal height: LighthouseFriends says the 1868 light was 75 ft above the lake; the USLHS place record gives 55 ft; the record has 23.0 m (75 ft). Not resolved; not in facts. (2) Characteristic: the record says Fl W 4s and Wikipedia says flashing white 4 s; LighthouseFriends gives a fixed-white light in 1856. The Light List was not opened (navcen 403), so the present characteristic is unverified and omitted. (3) Anderssen (1939-1941) appears in the roster after the 1934 discontinuance; the sources do not explain it. (4) The roster spells the keeper's name Tabberrah; LighthouseFriends uses Tabbarrah once. (5) Platt's 1838 report is quoted here as LighthouseFriends quotes it; the original was not read. (6) The 1814 battle is described from LighthouseFriends only. (7) The 1948 family is not named: they were private residents of a converted lighthouse. The 1996 buyer is not named. (8) Chronicling America searches for Cumberland Head and Tabberrah returned no local reporting of the station for 1868-1935 that we could read; the search is not exhaustive. (9) Lighthouse Board reports (1891-1900, in the corpus) list the light and a 1893 survey of its reservation, but the 1893 line is garbled by OCR, so it is not quoted. (10) The USCG Historian's page on Cumberland Head (archived copy) could not be read: the Wayback capture returned only its index. Its 'lens returned in 2003' and 'active aid' claims are not used. (11) Lighthouse Depot's database entry (replaced in 1934, moved back 2003) appeared in search results only; not read. (12) The USLHS roster and the Commissioner's 1921 list give Fido as keeper; the Commissioner's passage is on printed page 59 under 'Saving of life and property'; scan page 664. (13) The story no longer says work began in 1836: the source gives Congress's $5,000 and the land purchase in 1836, not a start of work. (14) 'On the same point' was changed to 'on the point': LighthouseFriends says the 1867 rebuild was on 'a more eligible site' and the old material went to 'a nearby location', so the same spot is not stated. (15) 'Judged more suitable' is replaced by LighthouseFriends' own words 'a more eligible site'; the source does not say who judged. (16) Verification pass 2026-10-28: the 1868 and 1838 footnote gaps, the Riley and 'stone tower abandoned' footnotes, and units (feet with metres; fifty rods about 250 m) were added.
